newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. criticises China plan to scrap HK legislature.
newsitem.headline: U.S. criticises China plan to scrap HK legislature.

text.p: The United States opposes moves by China to disband Hong Kong's elected legislature next year and is not satisfied at the progress of human rights talks with Beijing, the top U.S. diplomat on Asia said on Thursday.
"We believe that the disbanding of the elected legislature is both unnecessary and unwise," U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Winston Lord told reporters at the end of a two-day visit to Hong Kong.
"The United States has a very strong interest in seeing a smooth and successful transition here and will be working to support that process up to and through and beyond July 1, 1997."

China opposes democratic reforms brought in by British colonial Governor Chris Patten without its approval, and has vowed to replace the elected legislature with a provisional body when it takes over the territory in the middle of next year.

A Beijing-controlled Selection Committee is in the final stages of picking the man who will succeed Patten as the head of post-colonial Hong Kong and will name the 60-member interim legislature by the end of the month.

Lord met Patten and his deputy Anson Chan as well as members of the Legislative Council and the Trade Development Council. He also met Zhou Nan, head of Xinhua news agency's Hong Kong branch, China's de facto embassy in the British territory.

But it was his meeting with shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, frontrunner in the race for post-handover chief executive, that prompted criticism from the territory's pro-democracy camp, which said Washington appeared to be ordaining a winner ahead of the Selection Committee's decision, expected on December 11.
Lord said his meeting with Tung, who is an acquaintance of his wife, author Bette Bao Lord, was a personal visit with "no political significance".
"I've seen him on previous trips -- it would have been strange if I hadn't seen him on this trip," he said. "I would like to have seen all the candidates for chief executive if I'd had the time."
China and the United States have many issues of concern beyond the handover of Hong Kong.
Lord, who visited China in an unannounced trip in October, said Washington had raised the issue of human rights with Beijing frequently in talks but was looking for better progress.

"We are not satisfied with the progress on this issue and we will keep raising it. The full potential of our relationship with China cannot be realised until the human rights situation makes progress," Lord said.

In addition to human rights, Beijing and Washington have had differences over the annual review of China's Most Favoured Nation trading status, copyright protection and textile quotas. Also at issue is the US$35 billion trade surplus Beijing enjoys.

Beijing is lobbying to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) as a developing nation but has met with opposition from Western nations, especially the United States, which insist China's economy is too large for preferential treatment.

"Our position on the WTO will be on these economic and commercial grounds: Are they meeting our concerns of market access? Do they have a commercially meaningful offer?" Lord said. "We're not linking this to non-economic issues."
Lord stressed the U.S. had many common interests with China, including peace on the Korean peninsula, nuclear non-proliferation, the environment and regional security.
Lord, who is leaving government in January, said he was not likely to make another trip to China in an official capacity.
